latin.92: CAPVT IX. Declaratio doctrinae de Imputatione primi peccati, Ex Hebr. cap. 7. verf. 9. 10. de decimatione Levi in lumbis Abrahae, vocatur ad examen. I. Doctrinam de imputatione primi peccati antecedente seu immediata nullis Scripturae fundamentis innixam esse jam, opinor, patet. Num ea saltem illustrari possit, nam probari certe non potest, ex Hebr. vii. 9. 10. ubi dicitur Levi decimatus in lumbis Abrahae, paucis videamus. Ait D. G. Originalis peccati in nos ex Adamo transeuntis naturam & rationem ex hoc loco declarare Theologis solemne esse. Bene dixit originalis peccati: Nominat enim quosdam qui imputationem immediatam non modo non docent, sed aperte damnant. Possem ex Augustino, Bucero, Martyre, Gualtero, Gerhardo, &c. multa loca proferre: sed ne in re clara aequo longior videar, unius Anselmi his verbis ero contentus.
latin.93: Non portant (infantes qui non servantur) peccatum Adae sed suum. Nam aliud fuit peccatum Adae, aliud infantum, quia differunt ut dictum est. Illud enim fuit causa, istud est effectus. Et paulo post. Cum dicit Apostolus, quod supra posui, quia mors regnavit ab Adam usque ad Mosem, etiam in eos qui non peccaverunt in similitudinem praevaricationis Adae, sicut significat infantum minus esse quam Adae peccatum, ita aperte monstrat aliud esse. Quapropter cum damnatur infans pro peccato originali, damnatur non pro peccato Adae, sed pro suo. Nam si ipse non haberet suum peccatum, non damnaretur. Ita ergo non portat iniquitatem Adae sed suam, quamvis ideo dicatur portare, quia iniquitas illius peccati istius causa fuit.
latin.94: II. Sed quid ex decimatione Levi colligit D. Garissolius? Sicut, inquit, Abrahamus originarium fuit principium Gentis Leviticae, quae secundum rationem seminalem ab eo propagata est, ita & Adam principium est materiale totius generis humani, quod ad generationem naturalem attinet. Itaque si recte dictum est ab Apostolo Leviticos sacerdotes decimatos fuisse in Abrahamo, quia in ejus lumbis erant, quando scilicet Abrahamus Dei sacerdoti Melchisedeco decimas persolvit; nihil mirum videri debet, aut inusitatum, quod dicuntur omnes homines peccasse in Adamo, & in eo perditi ac damnati fuisse, quatenus omnes in ejus peccantis lumbis fuerunt. Quid vetat me hoc totum concedere, negantem imputationem primi Adae peccati actualis immediatam?
latin.95: Fayus certe verba ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον vertit in quo omnes peccaverunt, ut hoc, inquit, intelligatur de Adamo, cujus peccatum fuit commune omnium; sicut communis est omnium poena sive mors. Haec autem non imputatione communis est omnium, sed propagatione tantum. Idem ergo de peccato dicendum est. itaque illud omnes peccaverunt, exponit de peccato, quod non committitur actu, sed habitu quodam in nobis adhaeret. Et iterum alio loco. Peccaverunt autem in Adamo: sed non in similitudinem praevaricatoris Adami: quia non propter cupiditates suas peccarunt, quas in se nullas habebant, cum essent pueruli vel infantuli: ergo propter peccatum aliud a peccato Adae. qua de re in Arausicano concilio sic legitur, Injustitiam Deo dat qui mortem, quae est peccati poena, sine peccato, quod est meritum mortis, ad nos transiisse dicit. Dicantur ergo omnes homines peccasse in Adamo, modo id accipiatur de peccato habituali seu corruptione, quid hoc juvat imputationem antecedentem? Aut quid opus est ad talem illustrationem peccati originalis nobis nullo modo nocentem, nos respondere?
latin.96: Pertendit tamen Placeus in Thesibus de statu hominis lapsi ante Gratiam, non magis inde colligi Adami peccatum nobis imputari, quam colligi potest, aut peccata Abrahami, aut ejus fidem & bona opera eidem Levi imputata fuisse, quae tamen ei imputata fuisse nemo dixerit. Hoc confitetur D. Garissolius: Sed negat eo fine hoc Apostolicum Testimonium a tot & tantis Theologis in hoc negotio usurpari. Non enim, inquit, inde directe quisquam colligit Adami peccatum nobis imputari. Habet igitur Placeus quod voluit, imputationem immediatam (de qua sola eum agere patet ex Th. vii.) non posse probari ex hoc loco. Ille enim sic argumentabatur. Quae doctrina ad religionem spectans non potest probari ex sacris literis, ea est reijcienda. Doctrina de imputatione immediata inobedientiae actualis Adami non potest probari ex sacris literis. Ergo est reijcienda. Major non potest a Reformato vocari in dubium. Minor ab eo sic probabatur. Si quae sunt sacrae literae, ex quibus illa imputatio probari possit, illae petuntur praecipue ex cap. V. Epist. ad Rom. verf. 12. & seqq. & Hebr. vii. verf. 9. 10. Sed ex illis locis non potest illa imputatio probari. Ergo non potest probari ex sacris literis.
latin.97: Sed fortasse ex hoc loco colligere potest aliquis indirecte, peccatum Adami actuale nobis imputari immediate. Nam, inquit D. G. si quod fecit Abrahamus decimas dando, fecisse censentur tot postea seculis nati Levitae, nec tamen est in ejusmodi imputatione aliquid a ratione, aut Dei justitia alienum, nemo causam dicet, quare qui asserunt Adae peccatum censeri posterorum peccatum, ita ut in eo dicantur peccasse ac damnati fuisse, habendi sint pro absurditatum hamaxariis, aut rectae rationis & divinae justitiae adversariis. Rursus potest hoc totum concedi, absque ullo causae quam ago dispendio. Fateor enim Adae peccatum censeri posterorum peccatum ob vitium illis inhaerens ab eo derivatum. Fateor in eo dici posse posteros ejus peccasse ac damnatos fuisse, quia nimirum ab eo peccatum inhaerens & per peccatum damnationem suam traxerunt. Sed nego peccatum actuale Adami ita nobis omnibus ejus posteris imputari, ut ea imputatione nostrum fiat, alioqui non nostrum, & ut sic imputatum puniatur, corruptionem haereditariam, quae vere peccatum est, tanquam poenam proprie dictam, ac ut justitia fiat, infligi, nec-non mortem corporis & aeternam. Hoc est quod absurditatibus cumulamus, a quibus liberari non potest per decimationem Levi in Lumbis Abrahae. An enim ex eo quod decimatus dicitur Levi in Lumbis Abrahae, consequitur, imputationem illam posse probari ex sacris literis, non pugnare cum oraculo, Filius non feret iniquitatem Patris, non facere Deum autorem peccati, & Christum peccatorem &c.? Impedit-ne ne sint bona & solida argumenta, quibus imputationem illam oppugnamus? Nullo modo. Quid igitur imputationem illam juvat haec decimatio? Nihil prorsus. Vin' praeterea ostendam quam male ratiocinetur D. Garissolius?
latin.98: Si quis in praetereuntem rosas projiciat, nihil sequetur absurdi: hae enim minime nocent. An ergo similiter, si quis in praetereuntem lapides aut lutum projiciat, nihil sequetur absurdi? Se habet autem solutio decimarum ut rosa quae non potuit nocere Levi: At peccatum Adami non solum ut lapis, sed ut summum malum. Non fuerit igitur alienum a justitia, si solutio decimarum ab Abrahamo facta tribuatur Levi; quia id ei nullo modo nocuit, aut nocere potuit: An sequitur inde, non esse alienum a justitia, si peccatum ab Adamo commissum ejus posteris tribuatur, atque ita malum maximum illis inferatur? Non admodum opus est aliis responsionibus; quatuor tamen alias nobis D. Garissolius tribuit, quas fortasse ex Priore, quod vocat, Manuscripto exprompsit, & prolixe admodum refellere conatur, sed, pro suo more, conatu infoelici.

pass_a.92: Chapter IX opens. Its declared task is to call to examination the doctrine of the imputation of the first sin from Hebrews 7:9–10 on Levi being tithed in Abraham's loins. Head I: Placeus judges it already plain that the doctrine of antecedent or immediate imputation of the first sin rests on no Scriptural foundations. The remaining question is whether that doctrine can at least be illustrated — for it certainly cannot be proved — from Hebrews 7:9–10, where Levi is said to have been tithed in Abraham's loins; Placeus will look briefly. Opponent D. Garissoles (D. G., margin Cap. x. §1) says it is customary for theologians to declare from this locus the nature and reason of original sin passing into us from Adam. Placeus praises the phrase original sin: Garissoles is naming writers who not only fail to teach immediate imputation but openly condemn it. Placeus could produce many passages from Augustine, Bucer, Martyr, Gualther, Gerhard, and others; but lest he seem longer than fair in a clear matter, he will be content with Anselm's words alone.
pass_a.93: Anselm (De conceptu virginali et de originali peccato): infants who are not saved do not bear Adam's sin but their own. Adam's sin was one thing, the infants' another, because they differ as already said. Adam's was the cause; the infant's is the effect. A little later Anselm continues from the Apostle's words Placeus had cited: death reigned from Adam to Moses even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression (Romans 5:14). Just as that shows the infant's sin is less than Adam's, it also plainly shows it is another sin. Therefore when an infant is damned for original sin, he is damned not for Adam's sin but for his own. If he did not have his own sin, he would not be damned. So he does not bear Adam's iniquity but his own, even if he is said to bear it because that iniquity of Adam's was the cause of this sin of his.
pass_a.94: Head II: What then does Garissoles gather from Levi's being tithed? He says: as Abraham was the originative principle of the Levitical people, propagated from him by seminal relation, so Adam is the material principle of the whole human race as to natural generation. Therefore if the Apostle rightly said Levitical priests were tithed in Abraham because they were in his loins when Abraham paid tithes to Melchizedek, God's priest, it should seem neither strange nor unusual that all humans are said to have sinned in Adam and in him been ruined and damned, insofar as all were in the loins of him while he was sinning. Placeus asks what forbids him to concede that whole comparison while still denying the immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin.
pass_a.95: Fayus (Comm. on Romans 5) renders ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον as in whom all sinned, so that this is understood of Adam, whose sin was common to all, just as the penalty or death is common to all. But Placeus insists that commonality is by propagation only, not by imputation; the same must be said of the sin. So Fayus expounds all sinned of a sin not committed by act but adhering in us by a certain habit. Elsewhere Fayus: they sinned in Adam, yet not in the likeness of Adam the transgressor, because they did not sin from their own desires — which they did not have as little children or infants — and therefore on account of another sin than Adam's. On this the Council of Orange reads that whoever says death, the penalty of sin, passed to us without sin, which is the desert of death, attributes injustice to God. So let all be said to have sinned in Adam, provided that is taken of habitual sin or corruption: how does that help antecedent imputation? Or why must we answer an illustration of original sin that does us no harm at all?
pass_a.96: Still Placeus had already pressed the point in his Theses on fallen man before grace: the Levi text no more yields an imputation of Adam's sin to us than it would yield an imputation to Levi of Abraham's sins, or of Abraham's faith and good works — and nobody claims those were imputed to Levi. Garissoles grants that reading of the analogy, yet refuses the further claim that the many eminent theologians who cite the Apostolic testimony do so in order to prove direct imputation. His words: nobody draws from the place, directly, that Adam's sin is imputed to us. That confession hands Placeus the conclusion he sought. Immediate imputation — and Thesis vii shows that alone is under dispute — cannot be demonstrated from Hebrews 7:9–10. Placeus's own earlier syllogism was: a religious teaching that sacred Scripture cannot prove must be rejected; immediate imputation of Adam's actual disobedience is such a teaching; therefore reject it. Among the Reformed the major stands beyond dispute. The minor he secured by noting that the only passages usually alleged are chiefly Romans 5:12 and what follows, together with Hebrews 7:9–10; yet those very passages fail to prove the imputation; therefore sacred letters as a whole do not prove it.
pass_a.97: But perhaps someone can gather indirectly from this locus that Adam's actual sin is immediately imputed to us. Garissoles argues: if what Abraham did in paying tithes is reckoned done by Levites born so many ages later, and yet nothing in that kind of imputation is alien to reason or God's justice, nobody will explain why those who assert Adam's sin is reckoned the posterity's sin — so that in him they are said to have sinned and been damned — should be treated as carts of absurdities or as enemies of right reason and divine justice. Placeus again can concede the whole without cost to his cause. He grants Adam's sin is reckoned the posterity's because of the vice inhering in them derived from him. He grants posterity can be said to have sinned in him and been damned, because they drew inherent sin and thereby their damnation from him. But he denies that Adam's actual sin is so imputed to all his posterity that by that imputation it becomes ours (otherwise not ours), and that, being so imputed, it is punished by inflicting hereditary corruption — which truly is sin — as a penalty properly so called, and bodily and eternal death, as though justice required it. That is the heap of absurdities from which Levi's tithing in Abraham's loins cannot free the immediate view. Does Levi's being called tithed in Abraham's loins prove that imputation from sacred letters, prove it does not clash with the oracle The son shall not bear the father's iniquity, prove it does not make God author of sin and Christ a sinner, and so on? Does it block the good solid arguments by which Placeus attacks that imputation? Not at all. So what help is this tithing to that imputation? None whatsoever. Shall he show further how badly Garissoles reasons?
pass_a.98: If someone throws roses at a passer-by, nothing absurd follows, for roses barely harm. Does it follow likewise that if someone throws stones or mud at a passer-by, nothing absurd follows? Paying tithes stands like a rose that could not harm Levi; but Adam's sin stands not only like a stone but like the supreme evil. So it need not be alien to justice if Abraham's payment of tithes is attributed to Levi, because it neither harmed him nor could harm him. Does it follow that it is not alien to justice if the sin Adam committed is attributed to his posterity and so the greatest evil is inflicted on them? Other answers are scarcely needed; yet Garissoles assigns Placeus four further replies, perhaps drawn from what he calls the Prior Manuscript, and tries at great length to refute them — unhappily, as is his way. Placeus stops the opening block here before entering Responsio secunda.

92:
CAPUT IX. The doctrine of the imputation of the first sin is called to examination from Hebrews 7:9–10, on Levi being tithed in Abraham's loins.

I. That the doctrine of antecedent or immediate imputation of the first sin rests on no foundations in Scripture is already, I think, plain. Can it at least be illustrated — for it certainly cannot be proved — from Hebrews 7:9–10, where Levi is said to have been tithed in Abraham's loins? Let us see in a few words. D. Garissoles says it is customary for theologians to declare from this place the nature and reason of original sin as it passes into us from Adam. He said well, "of original sin": for he names certain writers who not only do not teach immediate imputation, but openly condemn it. I could bring forward many places from Augustine, Bucer, Martyr, Gualther, Gerhard, and others; but lest I seem longer than is fair in a clear matter, I will be content with these words of Anselm alone.
93: "They do not bear" — infants who are not saved — "Adam's sin, but their own. For Adam's sin was one thing, the infants' another, because they differ as has been said. That was the cause; this is the effect." And a little later: "When the Apostle says what I set down above, that death reigned from Adam to Moses even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression, just as he signifies that the infant's sin is less than Adam's, so he plainly shows that it is another. Therefore when an infant is damned for original sin, he is damned not for Adam's sin, but for his own. For if he himself did not have his own sin, he would not be damned. So then he does not bear Adam's iniquity, but his own — even if he is therefore said to bear it, because that iniquity of that sin was the cause of this."
94: II. But what does D. Garissoles gather from Levi's being tithed? "As," he says, "Abraham was the originative principle of the Levitical nation, which was propagated from him according to seminal relation, so also Adam is the material principle of the whole human race as far as natural generation is concerned. Therefore if the Apostle rightly said that the Levitical priests were tithed in Abraham because they were in his loins when Abraham paid tithes to Melchizedek, the priest of God, nothing strange or unusual ought to seem in the saying that all humans sinned in Adam and in him were ruined and damned, insofar as all were in the loins of him while he was sinning." What forbids me to grant this whole comparison, while still denying the immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin?
95: Fayus certainly renders the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον "in whom all sinned," so that this, he says, is understood of Adam, whose sin was common to all, just as the penalty or death is common to all. But this is common to all not by imputation, only by propagation. The same, then, must be said of the sin. And so he expounds that "all sinned" of a sin not committed by act, but adhering in us by a certain habit. And again elsewhere: "But they sinned in Adam — yet not in the likeness of Adam the transgressor — because they did not sin on account of their own desires, which they had none of in themselves when they were little children or infants; therefore on account of another sin than Adam's." On which matter the Council of Orange reads thus: "He attributes injustice to God who says that death, which is the penalty of sin, passed to us without sin, which is the desert of death." So let all humans be said to have sinned in Adam, provided that is taken of habitual sin or corruption: what help is that to antecedent imputation? Or what need is there for us to answer such an illustration of original sin, which does us no harm at all?
96: Yet Placeus pressed in the Theses on the state of fallen man before grace that one no more gathers from this that Adam's sin is imputed to us than one can gather that Abraham's sins, or his faith and good works, were imputed to the same Levi — which yet nobody will say were imputed to him. D. Garissoles confesses this; but he denies that so many and so great theologians use this Apostolic testimony in the present business for that end. "For," he says, "nobody gathers from it directly that Adam's sin is imputed to us." Placeus therefore has what he wanted: immediate imputation (and from Thesis vii it is plain he is treating that alone) cannot be proved from this place. For he had argued thus: Whatever doctrine belonging to religion cannot be proved from the sacred letters is to be rejected. The doctrine of the immediate imputation of Adam's actual disobedience cannot be proved from the sacred letters. Therefore it is to be rejected. The major cannot be called in doubt by a Reformed man. He proved the minor thus: If there are any sacred letters from which that imputation can be proved, they are sought chiefly from Romans 5:12 and following, and from Hebrews 7:9–10. But from those places that imputation cannot be proved. Therefore it cannot be proved from the sacred letters.
97: But perhaps someone can gather indirectly from this place that Adam's actual sin is immediately imputed to us. For, says D. Garissoles, if what Abraham did in giving tithes is reckoned done by Levites born so many ages later, and yet nothing in that kind of imputation is alien to reason or to God's justice, nobody will give a reason why those who assert that Adam's sin is reckoned the posterity's sin — so that in him they are said to have sinned and been damned — should be held for cartloads of absurdities, or for adversaries of right reason and divine justice. Again this whole can be granted without any loss to the cause I am pleading. For I confess that Adam's sin is reckoned the posterity's sin on account of the vice inhering in them, derived from him. I confess that his posterity can be said to have sinned in him and been damned, because from him they drew inherent sin and, through sin, their own damnation. But I deny that Adam's actual sin is so imputed to all of us his posterity that by that imputation it becomes ours — otherwise not ours — and that, being so imputed, it is punished by inflicting hereditary corruption, which truly is sin, as a penalty properly so called, and also the death of the body and eternal death, as though justice were to be done. This is what we heap with absurdities, from which we cannot be freed by Levi's being tithed in Abraham's loins. For from the fact that Levi is said to have been tithed in Abraham's loins, does it follow that that imputation can be proved from the sacred letters, that it does not clash with the oracle "The son shall not bear the father's iniquity," that it does not make God the author of sin and Christ a sinner, and so on? Does it hinder there being good and solid arguments by which we attack that imputation? In no way. What then does this tithing help that imputation? Nothing at all. Shall I show further how badly D. Garissoles reasons?
98: If someone throws roses at a passer-by, nothing absurd will follow: for these barely harm. Does it follow likewise that if someone throws stones or mud at a passer-by, nothing absurd will follow? But the payment of tithes stands as a rose that could not harm Levi; Adam's sin, however, stands not only as a stone, but as the supreme evil. It will not therefore have been alien to justice if the payment of tithes made by Abraham is attributed to Levi, because it neither harmed him nor could harm him. Does it follow from that that it is not alien to justice if the sin committed by Adam is attributed to his posterity, and so the greatest evil is inflicted on them? There is not much need of other replies; yet D. Garissoles assigns us four others, which he perhaps drew out of what he calls the Prior Manuscript, and tries at great length to refute — but, after his manner, with an unhappy attempt.
